Newborn Garden dormice are remarkably small, with a typical wet weight at birth of just 2 grams [Wwb = 2 grams] recorded in laboratory settings, though field-caught neonates have been documented at up to 2.5 grams. This altricial neonate mass represents a stark contrast to the species' ultimate adult body size, as reproductively mature individuals can reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 120 grams [Wwi = approximately 120 grams], a value that exceeds the widely cited AnAge database figure of 82.5 grams and likely reflects the higher quality diets available in captivity. The suckling juvenile undergoes a period of rapid mass gain before achieving nutritional independence, a developmental milestone marked by the cessation of milk ingestion. The dietary transition from lactation to solid food typically concludes relatively early in life, with the time since birth at weaning observed to be about 30 days [tx = about 30 days] under controlled thermal cond at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]itions. The physiological basis for this abbreviated nursing stage is thought to relate to the energetic demands placed on the lactating female during the temperate breeding season.

Reproduction in the Garden dormouse is comparatively modest in pace when viewed against the backdrop of other small-bodied glirids inhabiting Mediterranean ecosystems. Under optimal captive conditions maintained at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], females have been observed producing 1.2 litters each year [F_R_i = 1.2 litters each year], with each litter averaging 5 pups [N_R_i = averaging 5 pups]. The duration of each individual gestation period is tightly constrained by maternal physiology; at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the gestation time is approximately 23 days [tg = approximately 23 days], a relatively short interval among rodents of comparable body mass. This brief internal gestation is typical of altricial mammals, where considerable post-natal development must occur before the neonate can achieve independence. The synchrony between parturition and seasonal resource pulses, particularly the autumnal peak in arthropod and fruit availability, likely drives this specific reproductive schedule in wild populations inhabiting deciduous and mixed forest across southern and central Europe.

Sexual maturation in the Garden dormouse occurs well after the completion of somatic growth, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves before the onset of gonadal activity. Under standard thermoneutral conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the time since birth at puberty is reported to be approximately 365 days [tp = approximately 365 days], meaning that young born in the late summer cohort typically do not achieve reproductive maturity until the following autumn. This prolonged prepubertal interval contrasts with many other glirids, which may mature more quickly if environmental conditions permit an earlier first breeding event. The delay is ecologically meaningful insofar as it aligns the period of maximum energetic demand associated with lactation and pup rearing with the peak abundance of high-protein invertebrate prey available in temperate forests during the late spring. As such, the onset of reproductive activation corresponds closely with seasonal changes in day length and ambient temperature.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Garden dormouse under laboratory conditions, where extrinsic mortality factors such as predation are largely absent, has been estimated at around 5.5 years [am = around 5.5 years] at 37.5 °C at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This longevity is relatively extended for a rodent of its body mass and aligns with a slow-paced life-history syndrome characterized by modest annual fecundity and delayed maturation. In natural populations, however, senescence typically occurs far earlier due to the combined pressures of overwinter starvation, predation by nocturnal raptors and mustelids, and the physiological stress of hibernation. The species' ability to enter prolonged torpor during the cold months reduces daily energetic costs of tissue upkeep but also imposes a basal metabolic cost that must be met by autumn fat stores. The interplay between this hibernation strategy and the observed lifespan underscores the importance of thermal regulation in shaping the demographic trajectory of this small mammal.

Hibernation in the Garden dormouse involves profound reductions in metabolic rate and body temperature, during which the animals retreat to underground nests or rock crevices. The suite of developmental and reproductive metrics detailed above were all recorded under active-phase thermoneutral conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a temperature that corresponds to the species' normothermic core body temperature during the active season. Interpreting these life-history parameters in the context of the annual cycle is essential: the 365 days [tp = 365 days] to puberty effectively spans two active seasons separated by one hibernation period, meaning that actual ontogenetic development is compressed into a much shorter window of physiological activity at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Similarly, the 30 days [tx = 30 days] from birth to weaning must be completed entirely within the spring-summer active phase to ensure that the neonate accumulates sufficient body mass before the onset of winter torpor at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Comparative data from related glirids suggest that this developmental schedule is finely tuned to the phenology of food resources in temperate European woodlands.
